blocks.text: Structured Data, Unstructured Data, Tabular Data, and Time Series Data all covered the shape data can take once it already exists. Data Sources steps back to a more practical, earlier question: before a dataset has any shape to discuss at all, where did it actually come from, and what does that origin imply about how much it can be trusted.

This topic covers the major categories of data sources used in real machine learning projects, the tradeoffs between building on internal data versus reaching for external sources, the licensing and bias considerations that come with any external source, and why combining multiple sources requires keeping track of where each record actually came from.
1. The Major Categories of Data Sources

blocks.alt: The Major Categories of Data Sources
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442991147-901962466.png

Internal systems are the most common starting point for any organization already running a real product: databases, application logs, and transaction records that already exist because the business needs them for its own operation. Public datasets, such as Kaggle, the UCI Machine Learning Repository, and government open data portals, form a rich second category, often used for learning, benchmarking, or filling a gap internal data cannot cover.

APIs provide live, ongoing data from an external service, such as a weather API, a stock price feed, or a social media platform. Web scraping extracts data directly from public web pages when no clean API exists. Surveys and manual collection remain relevant when the needed information does not exist anywhere yet and has to be gathered directly from people. Sensors and IoT devices generate the continuous, high volume streams behind most of the time series data covered in the previous topic.

items: Internal systems: databases, application logs, and transaction records.
Public datasets: Kaggle, the UCI Machine Learning Repository, government open data.
APIs: live, ongoing data pulled from an external service.
Web scraping: extracting data directly from public web pages.
Surveys and manual collection: gathered directly from people.
Sensors and IoT devices: continuous, high volume real world streams.

blocks.text: 2. Internal Versus External Data
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992975-280819848.png

Internal data is the data your own organization already owns, generated by your own users, your own systems, your own processes. It is usually the most directly relevant data available, since it reflects your actual real world problem, but it is also limited to whatever you already happened to collect, and to whoever your existing users actually are.

External data broadens that picture considerably: a public dataset or an API can bring in information no internal system was ever built to capture. The tradeoff is real: external data usually comes with less control over its quality, less certainty about how it was originally collected, and licensing constraints that internal data never has to worry about.

blocks.text: 3. Licensing: An Easy Step to Skip and Regret

blocks.alt: Licensing: An Easy Step to Skip and Regret
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992977-997288629.png

Every external dataset comes with license terms, whether or not those terms are obvious at first glance, and skipping this check is one of the costlier mistakes a project can make later. A dataset released freely for academic research is not automatically cleared for a commercial product, and scraped website content is not automatically free to redistribute or train a commercial model on.

The safe habit is to check the license before building anything on top of a new external source, not after, since retroactively replacing a dataset a whole pipeline was already built around is far more expensive than checking its terms up front.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A dataset being publicly downloadable does not mean it is free to use for any purpose. Research licenses, non-commercial licenses, and full commercial licenses are different things, and the difference matters the moment a model trained on that data ships to real users.

blocks.text: 4. Every Source Carries Its Own Bias

blocks.alt: Every Source Carries Its Own Bias
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992977-441857909.png

No data source is a neutral, unbiased window onto the world, and it is worth being direct about this early. Internal logs reflect only your own existing users: if your product has never reached a particular group of people, your internal data never will either. Scraped web data reflects who writes online, which is not a representative sample of who exists in the world.

Surveys reflect only who chose to respond, and response patterns are rarely random: people with strong opinions in either direction tend to respond more than people with mild, indifferent ones. Recognizing the specific bias a source is likely to carry, before building anything on top of it, is an essential habit that connects directly to the Data Quality topic that follows this one.
5. A Worked Example: Combining Two Sources
A common real pattern is combining an internal source with an external one to build a richer dataset than either could provide alone.

This combined dataset is richer than either source alone: the internal purchase data now carries a demographic dimension the internal system never tracked. The merge only works because both sources share a common key, customer_id, which is exactly the requirement covered next.
6. Combining Multiple Sources
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992978-422141300.png

Merging data from two or more sources requires a shared key that means the same thing in both, such as a customer id, an email address, or a product code, something both sources agree on. Without a reliable shared key, combining sources produces a dataset that looks merged but is actually matching the wrong records together, a mistake that can be difficult to detect after the fact.

Even with a reliable key, combined sources often disagree in small but important ways: different date formats, different units, different category naming, all of which need to be reconciled before the combined dataset is usable, work that overlaps directly with the Data Quality topic next in this module.

blocks.text: 7. Tracking Where Every Record Came From

blocks.alt: Tracking Where Every Record Came From
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992978-977224338.png

Once multiple sources are combined, it becomes easy to lose track of which original source any given record actually came from, and that loss of traceability, often called provenance, becomes a real problem the moment something goes wrong. If a quality issue turns up later, tracing it back to its origin is far faster when every record still carries a tag identifying its source.

This is a simple habit to build in from the start, adding a source column when combining datasets, rather than a difficult one to retrofit after the fact, once records from different origins have already been blended together with no way to tell them apart.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Add a source column to every dataset before combining it with anything else. It costs almost nothing to add up front and can save real investigation time later when a data quality problem needs to be traced back to its origin.

blocks.text: 8. Data Sources Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Data Sources Versus What Comes Next
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992979-738416573.png

Knowing where data came from is the necessary first step toward answering a harder, related question: can this data actually be trusted. A perfectly sourced, well licensed dataset can still be riddled with missing values, incorrect entries, or inconsistent formatting, exactly the concerns the next topic addresses directly.

Data Quality picks up immediately where this topic leaves off, taking the sourced, combined data described here and asking what specifically could be wrong with it, and how to detect those problems before they quietly undermine a model trained on top of them.

items: Data comes from internal systems, public datasets, APIs, web scraping, surveys, and sensors.
Internal data is directly relevant but limited; external data is broader but harder to fully control.
Every external dataset carries license terms that must be checked before it is used.
Every source carries its own bias, reflecting who it was collected from.
Combining sources requires a shared key and consistent formats and definitions.
Tagging records with their original source preserves provenance, making later problems traceable.
